One thing I’ve started to appreciate about contract drafting is that a good agreement is not just about putting terms and conditions on paper. It’s about making sure both parties understand what they are agreeing to.

While learning about Service Agreements, I realised how important it is to clearly define the scope of services, payment terms, responsibilities, timelines, and termination conditions.

A small ambiguity in an agreement might not seem important at the beginning of a business relationship. But when expectations differ, that same ambiguity can become a source of confusion or even a dispute.

This made me realise that contract drafting is not simply about using legal language. It’s about anticipating possible misunderstandings and addressing them before they become problems.

As a law graduate beginning my professional journey, I’m interested in learning more about commercial contracts and how they work in real business environments, particularly in international and GCC markets where businesses operate across different jurisdictions.

headline: Associate Manager - Procurement transformation|Digital transformation| Procurement Operations leader| Process Excellence| GCC Growth|Ex-Medt
text:
A household cook in Bengaluru earning ₹40,000 a month—with a defined afternoon break, clear boundaries after 8 PM, and protected Sundays—while entry-level corporate roles asking for a degree and multi-channel execution still start around ₹30,000.
On the surface, it looks like a paradox. After 15 years leading procurement and operations inside Global Capability Centers, I see something much more fundamental: a textbook lesson in supply, demand, and true value creation.
In procurement, we spend our careers talking about total cost of ownership, criticality, and market scarcity. Yet we often forget to apply that same lens to talent and daily operations:

Immediate, non-negotiable value: Daily meals across multiple households are an essential, high-frequency service. When demand is high and reliable providers are scarce, pricing reflects real-world necessity—not a credential.

Clearer SLAs and boundaries: A defined afternoon window and zero "quick calls" on Sundays is essentially a well-enforced Service Level Agreement. In corporate operations, we preach work-life balance and focus time, yet our actual workflows often reward constant availability over output.

The degree vs. capability gap: A BTech or MBA opens doors, but in GCC operations and Source-to-Pay transformation, value comes from problem-solving, process ownership, and technology fluency. Paying entry-level rates for broad, unspecialized expectations creates high attrition—which is one of the costliest hidden expenses i

Saudi road tenders are putting more weight on what companies build in the Kingdom.

From 1 July 2027, Saudi Arabia’s Local Content and Government Procurement Authority will apply local content weighting in the financial evaluation of road construction and maintenance tenders with an estimated value of SAR 10 million or more. It will also require at least 40% local content at the company level. 

The company-level requirement is what makes this announcement significant. It brings decisions about Saudi teams, supplier relationships and delivery capability forward, well before a tender is issued.

For contractors and engineering partners in the road sector, the coming months are an opportunity to establish their local content baseline, complete certification and give Saudi partners a defined role in delivery. International specialists can contribute by helping build the engineering and technical capabilities needed to construct and maintain these assets in the Kingdom.

The strongest bidders will be able to show where they create value in Saudi Arabia and how that capability improves project delivery.

author: Mostafa Hassanein, CFA, IFQ, FMVA
headline: Growth needs the right capital, not just more of it | Valuation & M&A · Sukuk & securitisation · Project & asset finance
text:
M&A is becoming one of the most important exit routes for Saudi private companies.

The momentum is clear. 10 of the 11 Saudi startup exits MAGNiTT tracked in 2025 were acquisitions. Merger filings with the competition authority (GAC) rose 29% in the second quarter of this year.

Why M&A works for many private companies:

A sale needs one buyer who sees the value. A strategic buyer only has to believe it can make the business worth more, through costs, network or a licence it lacks. That's why it can pay for value other buyers can't see.

Structure closes the gap. Earn-outs, deferred payments and part-payment in shares let the seller keep upside for the value it believes in, while the buyer pays upfront only what it can defend.

The buyers are already here. Many of the 2023 to 2025 IPO class raised capital and now need growth. Fakeeh Care, listed in 2024, completed a SAR 1.6bn cash purchase of a 350-bed Riyadh hospital in July. ADES, listed in 2023, completed a SAR 1.07bn purchase of a rig fleet this year.

My view: in 2027, I'd expect M&A to set many of the reference prices for Saudi late-stage companies, working alongside the IPO market rather than instead of it.

If you hold a pre-IPO stake, is a strategic sale part of your exit plan?

Sources: MAGNiTT, GAC, EnterpriseAM, Jawlah (links in the first comment).

Views are my own. Not investment advice.

author: Fahad Lateef (FCCA)
headline: Chairman @ Legend Group | Building 8 Companies Across Multiple Industries & Countries | Entrepreneur | FCCA
text:
The Saudi riyal and UAE dirham are pegged to the US dollar.

But neither is pegged to the British pound.

And that matters for UK businesses operating in the Gulf.

The Saudi riyal is fixed at SAR 3.75 per US dollar, while the UAE dirham has a central parity of AED 3.6725.

So, if your business earns in riyals or dirhams but pays its costs in pounds, movements in sterling can directly affect your margins.

A stronger pound means your Gulf revenue converts into fewer pounds. A weaker pound means more.

Of course, the actual exposure depends on where your costs sit and whether you have hedged your currency risk.

This is why I believe currency strategy should be part of the commercial conversation before signing an international contract.

Consider your pricing, costs, payment terms and exchange-rate exposure.

Winning business internationally is important. Protecting the profit you make from it is just as important.

Eligible applicants can receive residency for themselves and their families, dependent fee exemptions, visa-free exit and re-entry, business and property ownership rights, and exemption from the Nitaqat programme during the first three operating years.

author: Clayton Hayward
headline: Co-Founder @ Tharvos
text:
R100 million won't build an AI economy. It's a starting point.

President Ramaphosa came back from Silicon Valley backing a R100m AI startup fund. Credit to the founders who put it on the table.

Now look at what everyone else is doing:

Strive Masiyiwa Cassava Technologies is looking to raise up to US$1 billion, mostly for NVIDIA GPUs (Bloomberg). That's about R17.5 billion, 175 times our fund.

Saudi Arabia's National Infrastructure Fund has committed up to US$667m for AI compute and power.

Stargate's backers have announced plans to invest US$500 billion.

We're measuring in millions Zar. They're measuring in billions $$.

I've spent 30 years building fintech and payments businesses in Africa, and I'm now building AI-native companies here. Founders don't need slogans. They need three things:

Compute they can afford

Capital to scale, not just to start

A real path to their first big customers here at home, including government, banks and state-owned companies

Without all three, our best AI founders will do what too many great founders have done before: build here, then scale somewhere else….,

The real test of South Africa's AI ambition is how many globally competitive AI companies can afford to build and scale from here. A conference won't tell us that.

R100m is seed money for one venture. 

Where's the plan for the real investment needed ? 

Founders, investors, policymakers: what would you fund first?

#AI #SouthAfrica #Startups #VentureCapital #AfricaTech

Pay: SAR 120,000
GOSI at 12.75%: SAR 15,300
End of service: SAR 5,000

author: Mostafa Hassanein, CFA, IFQ, FMVA
headline: Growth needs the right capital, not just more of it | Valuation & M&A · Sukuk & securitisation · Project & asset finance
text:
M&A is becoming one of the most important exit routes for Saudi private companies.

The momentum is clear. 10 of the 11 Saudi startup exits MAGNiTT tracked in 2025 were acquisitions. Merger filings with the competition authority (GAC) rose 29% in the second quarter of this year.

Why M&A works for many private companies:

A sale needs one buyer who sees the value. A strategic buyer only has to believe it can make the business worth more, through costs, network or a licence it lacks. That's why it can pay for value other buyers can't see.

Structure closes the gap. Earn-outs, deferred payments and part-payment in shares let the seller keep upside for the value it believes in, while the buyer pays upfront only what it can defend.

The buyers are already here. Many of the 2023 to 2025 IPO class raised capital and now need growth. Fakeeh Care, listed in 2024, completed a SAR 1.6bn cash purchase of a 350-bed Riyadh hospital in July. ADES, listed in 2023, completed a SAR 1.07bn purchase of a rig fleet this year.

My view: in 2027, I'd expect M&A to set many of the reference prices for Saudi late-stage companies, working alongside the IPO market rather than instead of it.

If you hold a pre-IPO stake, is a strategic sale part of your exit plan?

Sources: MAGNiTT, GAC, EnterpriseAM, Jawlah (links in the first comment).

Views are my own. Not investment advice.

text:
Many private credit firms reportedly see Saudi Arabia as an estimated $100bn opportunity. Deploying capital at the required scale and speed is proving difficult.

Regulatory uncertainty, licensing timelines and rules on local presence are slowing the flow of capital, according to more than a dozen fund managers. Licensing a local fund can take up to a year, and at least six managers said raising money for local deals had become harder. Saudi Arabia's Capital Market Authority did not respond to a request for comment.

One example: a $150m financing for a little-known Saudi firm, backed by Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Fortress and at least three regional fund managers, took months. People familiar with the matter said it would have taken weeks in many other markets.

Deal size is part of the problem. Benefit Street Partners estimates about 60% of regional private credit deals are below $30m. At $50m a deal, the estimated $100bn would take 2,000 deals, by LPGP calculation.

The pay-off could be higher yields: as much as 16% or more, roughly twice the levels in more established markets, according to Franklin Templeton's Dino Kronfol, reflecting additional risks, smaller fund sizes and more concentrated positions.

For LPs and GPs: partnerships between international managers and local funds are one way to bridge the gap. Worth watching: licensing times, and whether each deal that closes makes the next one easier.
